name: Feedback Students Actually Use
title: Feedback Students Actually Use
answer: Feedback Students Actually Use is the idea that giving more feedback only matters if students act on it, and that AI can help teachers produce more feedback but not necessarily better feedback. It matters because students often ignore feedback entirely, and because students judge feedback by who they believe wrote it rather than by its quality.

sections.body: Feedback is one of the strongest tools a teacher has, and AI can increase the amount of it a teacher is able to give. The problem is that volume alone does not produce learning, since feedback only helps when it is good and when students actually use it. Research comparing human and AI feedback suggests human feedback is still better in most respects, so AI is not a simple replacement. The deeper problem is student behaviour, because many students receive feedback and change nothing in response. This idea asks teachers to think about feedback as something that must be designed to be used, not just delivered.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the text suggests AI may be most useful for early drafts, with teachers saving their own detailed feedback for later drafts where it matters most. This applies across grade bands, since the study of more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12 found similar rates of ignoring feedback across grades and task types. Teachers can therefore use AI to give quick responses on first attempts and reserve their own attention for the work that follows. Because students judge feedback by who they believe wrote it, how feedback is presented also becomes part of the planning. The aim is to arrange feedback so that students read it and then revise.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research findings. A meta analysis of 20 studies found a medium sized effect of automated writing feedback on students' writing performance (Fleckenstein et al., 2023), though results varied widely across studies. A study comparing 200 pieces of feedback from trained teachers with 200 from ChatGPT on secondary essays found humans gave higher quality feedback in every category except alignment with criteria (Steiss et al., 2024). Another study found AI and human feedback had similar quality overall, with both weak at helping students think about their own learning (Nazaretsky et al., 2026). In a study of more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, nearly half did not change a single character of their writing after receiving AI feedback (Jansen et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Human feedback remains better in most ways, so AI should not be treated as an equal substitute for teacher judgement. Students may dismiss good feedback they think came from AI or trust poor feedback they think came from a teacher, which means presentation and trust are risks to manage. Both AI and human feedback were found weak at helping students think about their own learning, so that work stays with the teacher. The decision about which drafts receive AI feedback and which receive detailed teacher feedback remains a professional choice, and feedback that students never use cannot help them.
